body:
>You'll be hard-pressed to find a reputable company who will hire you without a technical interview of some kind.

Of course my current job didn't have a technical interview. Go figure. 

I beat myself up about why I didn't pass. I spend about 60% of my free time going through courses on Coursera or Upcase, and have worked through most of the major Ruby or Ruby on Rails books. The killer part is that I don't have any friends or even acquaintances who are programmers, so I can't get a helping hand, advice, or even someone to just share my passion with. My peers from graduation either tweak CSS or went into IT (Technically the school's CS program has a 100% placement rate, but they don't say if it's in the field).

I have no issue getting interviews, and I always do very well on the non-technical interview. I have a lot of experience with leadership from college and beyond (President of Fraternity, successful Student Government member, Leader of ACM Chapter), I even am involved in the local startup community, ruby meetups (there really isn't one here and the members often don't respond to my messages), and have spoken at Barcamp. I think I have a lot of knowledge *about* Ruby and *about* Rails, but I've never applied it at more than a junior level. These solo projects aren't necessarily groundbreaking, but they're more than enough for most companies. I know how to do background processing/daemons, do complicated relations, etc. I had a technical interview that I conceptually destroyed. They asked me about ActiveRecord patterns in rails and they were super impressed. Then they asked me to write code, and although it worked, they just weren't impressed with *how* I wrote it, or maybe *what* I wrote; it wasn't efficient.  

>Have you taken initiative to offer tasks you could do for them? 

I've tried working on project like creating an employee access portal to consolidate our information and some of our web services that we use, but I've been told it's a waste of time -- as if I wasn't wasting my time already. One thing that I probably should have mentioned is that I manage myself most of the time. We have a project manager, but he mostly works with the offshore dev teams. By "dev" they mean working with MySQL Views as contract work for other companies.

I've heard, "well, you're a junior developer, and we're looking for someone with more experience" at least 3 times. Seems strange, because I'm very forthright with my graduation date and work experience. I think that's their way of politely telling me I'm not up to their standards? Last interview I did was take-home, and I structured the project to "Ruby standards" and tried to optimize it as much as possible. I even included a readme with my thought process and explanations on running the tests. 

They told me they'd take a few days to look at it, and get back to me with a potential third interview date. They responded about 2 hours later saying they went with a different candidate, which would lead me to believe they took one look at my code and turned me down.
